name: Ars Electronica Center
label: Ars Electronica
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Lentos Kunstmuseum' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Lentos Kunstmuseum Linz' (way/13959723): middle (152 m across); moved 15 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OSM W31340724 (Ars Electronica Center): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Museum of the Future by the Danube, lit with colours at night.

text.description:
The Ars Electronica Center is the big modern building on the Danube in Linz, and it is a straightforward subject for a phone camera. Seen from across the river, it gives you a wide, clear view of the whole building with water in front of it, which is what makes the picture work. A dependable view is from the promenade in front of the Lentos Kunstmuseum on the south bank. Guides describe the opposite-bank view from there as the most dependable one. The glass facade of Lentos is also often recommended for river reflections, so you can include the water, or the glass, as part of the shot.

If you want a different angle, two other places are suggested. Nibelungenbrücke gives a straight-on, centred view of the full facade across the Danube. Ars-Electronica-Straße shows the building head-on from the front, and at dusk you can catch car and tram light trails passing in front of it.

People pass along the promenade and the bridge, so take a moment to check the edges of the frame before you press the button. Exact spots can vary, so walk a few steps either way until the building sits neatly in the frame. Photo rules inside the building vary by exhibition, so ask before you take pictures indoors.
text.geographic_location: In Linz, on the banks of the Danube, with the viewing promenade on the opposite bank in front of the Lentos Kunstmuseum.
text.directions_text: No tram or railway stops are listed for this spot. From there the Ars Electronica Center lies about 340 m to the north-west, across the river. Look across the river towards it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x), which gives a natural view of the building across the water. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of river and sky, and keep the building away from the edges so it does not stretch. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a tighter crop of the facade.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Lentos Kunstmuseum (south bank of the Danube, on the promenade in front of the museum). The Ars Electronica Center on the opposite bank, with the river and reflections in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the water in the lower third, with the building across the middle of the frame. Keep the horizon level. If you want a straight-on, centred view of the full facade, try Nibelungenbrücke instead. Ars-Electronica-Straße is the alternative for a head-on shot with light trails at dusk.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright. At dusk, switch on night mode and rest your elbows on a railing to keep the phone steady, especially for the light trails.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Dusk is a good time because of the car and tram light trails near the building. In daylight, a calm day gives the clearest reflections on the water.

text.access_note: The riverside promenade and viewpoints are public; the building's interior and roof terrace are not free public viewpoints, so check the official site before you go.

name: Pöstlingberg
label: Pöstlingberg
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Franz-Josef-Warte' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Franz-Josefs-Warte' (way/89768110): middle (9 m across); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/101609056: the OpenStreetMap point 'Pöstlingberg'.
notes: Hilltop pilgrimage church with the best panorama over Linz.

text.description:
Pöstlingberg is Linz's own hill: a 539-metre rise on the left bank of the Danube, topped by the pilgrimage church and a viewing platform over the city. It is also home to the Linz Grottenbahn, and the mountain tramway (line 50 of the Linz tramway, running over the Pöstlingbergbahn) carries visitors up from the city centre. Most people photograph the view from the top. This spot flips that around and shows the hill itself, which makes a calmer picture than the busy tram-side angles.

The Franz-Josef-Warte is a lookout tower in Freinberg park. From the tower's wooden steps you see Pöstlingberg framed across the trees, with the green of Freinberg around it. The trees give you a natural frame, and the hill sits as a calm backdrop. It is a quieter, on-foot alternative to the crowded viewpoints.

For a second angle, try the Nibelungenbrücke over the Danube. It gives a wider frame with the hill across the river and the Urfahr side of the city beneath it. Check on the day for the best standing spot on the bridge. Keep your phone steady against the railing or a post, and wipe the lens before you shoot.
text.geographic_location: Pöstlingberg rises on the left (north) bank of the Danube in Linz. The viewpoint is the Franz-Josef-Warte lookout tower in Freinberg park.
text.directions_text: Start from the centre of Linz and head for Freinberg park. The tower is reached on foot within the park. Once you are on the tower's steps, Pöstlingberg is to the north. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the hill and the trees around it. Then try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the church-topped summit closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Franz-Josef-Warte. The hill of Pöstlingberg framed across the trees from the lookout tower's wooden steps, with the rest of the Freinberg greenery around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the hill on one of the upper lines, letting the tree branches form a frame at the edges. If you want a different view, the Nibelungenbrücke shows the hill across the Danube with Urfahr beneath it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the hill to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky does not wash out. Take a few shots at 1x and at a zoom setting, then pick the best.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters the hill and the trees. Go on a clear day so the hill stands out from the sky.

text.access_note: The tower is in Freinberg park; check for access rules or opening times before you go.

name: Lentos Art Museum
label: Lentos
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Ernst-Koref-Promenade' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Ernst-Koref-Promenade nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/13959723: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Lentos Museum of Modern Art' (152 m across).
notes: Glass-fronted modern art museum on the Danube.

text.description:
Lentos is Linz's museum of modern art, and the building is as much of a draw for photographers as the paintings inside. It opened in May 2003 and was designed by the Zurich firm Weber & Hofer. It is a long, low block about 130 metres from end to end, wrapped in a transparent glass façade. The glass is lit up after dark. It sits right on the Danube, between the Nibelungen Bridge and the Brucknerhaus, so you can pair the clean lines of the building with open sky and water.

Inside, the collection grew from works by Klimt, Schiele and Kokoschka, among others. That makes it a good stop if you like art as well as pictures of buildings.

From the promenade in front of the main glass façade, the building's repeated lettering and the reflections of sky and river do most of the work for you. Shoot it straight-on for tidy lines, or stand at an angle so the glass picks up more of the surroundings. If you want a wider view, the Nibelungenbrücke gives a long look along the Danube with the museum framed against the river and city. Down on the Donaulände, a lower and quieter angle puts the glass and the water in one frame. Keep your phone level and watch for your own reflection in the glass.
text.geographic_location: Lentos stands directly on the Danube in Linz, on the Ernst-Koref-Promenade, between the Nibelungen Bridge and the Brucknerhaus.
text.directions_text: No tram or railway stop is listed for this spot, so start from the Nibelungen Bridge or the Brucknerhaus, which are the two landmarks either side of the museum. Getting there by taxi or hired scooter is simplest: ask for the Lentos Art Museum on the Ernst-Koref-Promenade. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a straight-on view of the glass front. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you cannot fit the long building in, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the lettering and reflections.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Ernst-Koref-Promenade (in front of the main glass façade). The museum's transparent glass front and its repeated lettering, shot straight-on or at an angle to capture reflections of the sky and river. The museum lies to the north-west of you from here.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the roof edge up with a horizontal line so the building does not lean. Move a few steps sideways to change what the glass reflects. If you want a wider view, the Nibelungenbrücke gives a longer look along the Danube with the museum, river and skyline together. Check the bridge approach on arrival, as building work for a new walking and cycling ramp has been reported there.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the glass to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour. After dark, use night mode and hold the phone against a railing or your body to keep it steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go in daylight for sky and river reflections, then stay into the evening when the façade is lit. The night lighting is reported to change colour, so the look varies from night to night.

text.access_note: The promenade outside is open public space; the museum itself may have ticket and opening rules, so check the official site before you go.

name: Brucknerhaus
label: Brucknerhaus
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Donaupark' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Wohnen beim Donaupark' (way/108812913): middle (423 m across); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/13978207: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Brucknerhaus' (111 m across).
notes: Concert hall in the Danube park, home of the Bruckner Festival.

text.description: The Brucknerhaus is Linz's concert and congress hall, named after the composer Anton Bruckner. It was designed by the Finnish architects Heikki and Kaija Siren and built between 1969 and 1973. It opened in March 1974 with the Vienna Philharmonic under Herbert von Karajan. It hosts about 200 performances a year and is the home of the Brucknerfest and the Linzer Klangwolke. For photographers, the draw is the curved glass front that faces the Danube. From the riverside park you can show the whole building with grass, trees and water in the same frame, which makes a calm, uncluttered picture. The building is a long, low shape, so a wide shot works better than a close one. Keep the phone level, using gridlines, so the horizontal lines of the roof and glass stay straight. Tap on the building to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the glass keeps some detail. If you want a different angle, the Nibelungenbrücke gives a long view along the river towards the riverside frontage. The Schlossbergpark gives a wider city view from above, but it needs a walk uphill.
text.geographic_location: The Brucknerhaus stands beside the Danube in Linz, at the edge of the Donaupark. The park lies between the Nibelungenbrücke and the railway bridge.
text.directions_text: From the centre of Linz, head to the Donaupark on the riverside between the Nibelungenbrücke and the railway bridge. If you want to walk up to the building afterwards, it is about 8 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole building. If you cannot fit the full width in, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x). Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the curve of the glass, but keep the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Donaupark (riverside park between the Nibelungenbrücke and the railway bridge). The Brucknerhaus's curved glass front and building from the park side, with the Danube close by. The building is to the west of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the building along the lower third of the picture, with the sky above and some lawn or trees in front. Switch on gridlines and line them up with the roof and the base of the glass so the lines stay straight. For a second view, walk to the Nibelungenbrücke and shoot along the river towards the riverside frontage, with passing boats in the foreground if there are any.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is washing out. Avoid portrait mode for the building itself. Panorama can work if you cannot fit it in with the ultra-wide, but move slowly and keep the phone upright.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Evening, when the building is lit inside, can look especially striking, so try night mode for a steadier, brighter shot. Check the weather first, as the glass and the river reflect the sky.

text.access_note: The Donaupark is an open public park; entry to the Brucknerhaus itself depends on events, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The Donaupark is an open public space with no entry charge.
The building looks especially striking in the evening when the interior is lit (based on one visitor review).
Night mode and the exposure slider will help with evening and bright-sky conditions.
A telephoto lens (2x-5x) will help with detail shots from the stand-here point.

name: Hauptplatz Linz
label: Hauptplatz
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).
pin_note: Position from OSM W1551992348 (Stadtoase Hauptplatz Linz): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: The huge baroque main square, one of the largest enclosed squares in Europe.

text.description:
Hauptplatz Linz is a square in Linz, and it is a good place to practise a few easy phone shots. The open space lets you step back and fit the buildings around the edge into one frame, and the people crossing the square give the scene some life. You can take wide, airy pictures here without needing a special viewpoint.

The phone icon on the map is about 150 m north-west of the subject. That is a short stroll, so you can walk towards it and try a few positions on the way. Start wide to show the whole space. Then move closer and look for details: the fronts of the buildings, the paving, a café table, a passer-by.

Keep the phone level so the building edges stay straight. Switch on the gridlines to help with this. If the square is busy, wait a moment for a gap in the crowd, or use people as part of the picture and let them add scale. Wipe the lens with a soft cloth before you start, because a smudge shows up badly on pale buildings and sky.

The square is a pleasant place to pause, so build in some time to look around before you start shooting. Take one wide picture, one medium picture and one close detail, and you will have a good small set from this single stop.
text.geographic_location: Hauptplatz Linz is the square the map marks in Linz.
text.directions_text: No tram or railway stop is listed for this spot. From there the square is about 149 metres to the south-east, about 2 minutes on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 150 m north-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the width of the square and the buildings around it. Use the default lens (1x) for natural-looking shots and for people. Try telephoto/zoom (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for façade details and for candid shots of people crossing the square.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 150 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east. This is a short walk, about 2 minutes on foot. Take your first wide picture from the edge of the square, so the open space stretches out in front of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the building edges with the vertical lines so they do not lean. Keep some open paving in the foreground for depth, and put one building or a group of people on a third of the frame. Take a second shot at the default lens (1x) from a little further along for variety.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest building to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky turns white. Use portrait mode only when a person is close to you. For a wide sweep of the square, try panorama and move slowly and steadily.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Visit in the morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer and the square is likely to be less crowded. If you come after dark, use night mode and rest your elbows on something steady.

text.access_note: The square appears to be an open public space, but check the official site before you go in case of events or restrictions.

name: New Cathedral, Linz
label: Mariendom
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Franz-Josefs-Warte' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Franz-Josefs-Warte' (way/89768110): middle (9 m across); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/13961069: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'St. Mary's Cathedral' (147 m across).
notes: Austria's largest neo-Gothic church with tall stained glass windows.

text.description:
The New Cathedral (the Mariendom) is a neo-Gothic church and the largest church building in Austria. Building began with the first stone in 1862 and the cathedral was consecrated in 1924. Its tower reaches 134.6 m, which is two metres lower than the south tower of St Stephen's in Vienna. The originally planned spire was not approved, because no building in Austria-Hungary was allowed to be taller. Inside, the stained glass is well known, especially the Linz Window, which tells the story of the city.

This view looks at the cathedral from above, from the Franz-Josefs-Warte on the Freinberg ridge. Seen from a height, the tall tower and steep roofline stand out clearly against the rooftops, which is hard to do from the streets beside it. The tower's small platforms and the nearby clearings give you a few different angles to try.

The cathedral is quite far away, so use the telephoto lens to bring it closer rather than cropping later. If you want a different picture, the north bank of the river at Urfahr shows the cathedral across the water, with the old town, the castle and the Lentos museum in the same view.
text.geographic_location: The viewpoint is on the Freinberg ridge, on the western side of Linz, looking across the city to the cathedral to the east.
text.directions_text: Check a local transit map for the best way to reach the Freinberg ridge. The final approach to the tower is on a dirt and gravel path, so wear shoes with a good grip. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the telephoto lens (2x-5x, depending on your phone), because the cathedral is a long way off. The default lens (1x) works for a wide view of the city and river with the cathedral as a small part of it. Skip the ultra-wide (0.5x), which will make the cathedral very small.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Franz-Josefs-Warte (Freinberg ridge, on the tower's small platforms and nearby clearings). The Mariendom seen from above on the Freinberg ridge, with the city, the Danube and the surrounding hills behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the tower and roof in the upper-middle of the frame and let the city and river fill the space below. Switch on gridlines to keep the horizon level. If trees are in the way, move to one of the nearby clearings for a cleaner line. For the other classic view, the Urfahr riverside path on the north bank shows the cathedral across the river with the old town and castle.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the cathedral to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky does not wash out and the stonework keeps its detail. Hold the phone steady against the railing or your body when zoomed in. Take a few shots in case one is blurred.

text.access_note: Upper tower levels at the Franz-Josefs-Warte may be closed, and the cathedral itself is a place of worship, so check the official site for entry details before you go.

name: Linz Musiktheater
label: Musiktheater
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).
pin_note: Position from OSM W27206426 (Musiktheater Linz): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Modern opera house with a striking auditorium.

text.description:
The Linz Musiktheater is a theatre building in Linz, and it is a good stop if you like photographing buildings. Buildings with straight lines and wide surfaces suit a phone, because the shapes stay clear even in a quick snap.

You will be too near to fit everything in at the default lens (1x), so switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) and tilt the phone upwards a little. Switch on the gridlines and line them up with the edges of the building. That keeps the verticals straight and the picture looking calm and tidy.

For a second picture, step back as far as is comfortable and use the default lens (1x) to take in more of the front. Then use 2x or the telephoto to pick out a detail such as a window pattern, an entrance or a reflection. If people are passing, wait a moment and let them walk through the frame; a few figures give a good sense of scale. Check the official site for opening and visiting information before you go if you want to see inside.
text.geographic_location: The Linz Musiktheater stands in the city of Linz.
text.directions_text: Search for "Linz Musiktheater" on your map app and head there. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x), because the phone icon on the map is very close to the building. Use the default lens (1x) from further back, and the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the edges of the building up with them so the verticals stay straight. Keep the phone level before you tilt it up. Try one wide shot and one close detail shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the façade does not wash out.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft daylight, in the morning or late afternoon, is kinder to large surfaces than harsh midday sun. After dark, try night mode with the phone held steady against something solid.

text.access_note: Check the official site for opening and visiting information before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Soft morning or late-afternoon light is usually kinder to large façades than harsh midday sun.

name: Pöstlingbergbahn
label: Pöstlingbergbahn
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Hauptplatz' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Hauptplatz' (relation/1934891): middle (254 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/150353: large area '50: Pöstlingberg – Hauptplatz' (3039 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: One of the steepest adhesion tramways in the world, climbing to Pöstlingberg.

text.description:
The Pöstlingbergbahn is a narrow-gauge electric mountain tramway that climbs from Linz's main square up to the Pöstlingberg, the hill at the northern end of the city. It opened in 1898 and ran for over a century from a station in Urfahr. In 2009 it was extended to the Hauptplatz and joined to the city tram network, so the stop on the square is now the easiest place in town to see it. With a maximum gradient of 11.6%, it is the steepest railway of its kind in Austria, which is a good story to have in mind when you take the picture.

The photo works because of the contrast: a small tram in front of the square's historic buildings, with a bit of city life around it. Wait for a tram to pull in or move off rather than shooting an empty rail. If you want the summit end instead, the Grottenbahn station near the top is a good alternative, because the tram can be framed arriving or departing with that station nearby.

The old open-sided 'summer cars' were part of the line from the start, and the operator runs nostalgic open cars in summer only, so a vintage-tram shot depends on the season. Take a few frames as the tram approaches, because trams move faster than you expect.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Linz, on or beside the Hauptplatz (the main square), near the Pöstlingbergbahn stop. The line runs from here to the Pöstlingberg hill at the northern end of the city.
text.directions_text: Make your way to the Hauptplatz, the main square in the centre of Linz, where the line starts. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the tram with the square behind it. Switch to 0.5x if you want more of the historic buildings, and to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a closer, tighter tram shot from the edge of the square.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Hauptplatz (Pöstlingbergbahn stop on the square). The tram leaving from its city-centre stop, with the Linz square and its historic buildings as backdrop. The Pöstlingbergbahn line lies to the north-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the tram on one of the vertical lines so the buildings fill the rest of the frame. Keep the rails or overhead wires leading into the picture. For a different view, the Grottenbahn near the summit station shows the tram arriving or leaving with the station beside it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tram to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the buildings keep their colour. Hold the shutter button for a burst, or use Live Photos, so you can pick the best frame as the tram moves.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Check the timetable and aim for a moment when a tram is due. In summer you may be able to catch the nostalgic open cars, which the operator runs only in that season.

text.access_note: The Hauptplatz is an open public square, but tram timetables and tickets for the line and the summit attractions can change, so check the official site before you go.

name: Linz Castle
label: Linz Castle
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Schlosspark' (1 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Schlosspark' (pois).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/14039464: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Linz Castle' (187 m across).
notes: Hilltop castle above the Danube with views over the old town.

text.description:
Linz Castle sits on a hill above the old town, right beside the Danube, so it is easy to place in a photo with the river and the city around it. Its look is mixed: heavy old walls and a deep moat on one side, and a modern glass-and-steel south wing facing the city. That wing replaced one lost in the great city fire of 1800 and was finished in 2009. The site is much older. A Roman fort once stood here, and the first written mention of the castle dates from 799. Emperor Frederick III lived here from 1489 to 1493, and the main block you see today goes back to a rebuilding ordered by Emperor Rudolf II around 1600. Today it houses a museum.

For a good phone photo, go to the Schlosspark, the green area behind the castle. From there the castle sits in the frame with the Danube, a bridge and a wooded slope in front of it. Boats on the river, such as freight ships, can add a sense of place if one passes. Start with the default lens (1x) and use the gridlines to keep the river level. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the slope and water around the castle. Use 2x or more to pick out the castle itself. If you have time, the north bank of the river and the Burggraben (the castle moat) give quite different views of the same building.
text.geographic_location: Linz Castle stands on a hill above the old town of Linz, directly on the Danube. The Schlosspark lies behind it, to the west.
text.directions_text: There is no tram or station stop at this spot, so start in the old town of Linz and head up the hill to the castle. Once there, turn east to see the castle in your frame. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the castle with the river and slope around it. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the foreground slope, bridge and water as well. Try 2x or more to pick out the castle walls and the glass wing from a distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Schlosspark. A Danube view with the castle in the frame, with a freight ship, the bridge and a wooded slope in the foreground, shown in a sunset example photo. A freight ship on the river makes a good extra subject if one passes.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and set the horizon of the river on a lower line. Keep the castle on one side of the frame and the river and bridge on the other. Use the wooded slope as a dark foreground to give depth. For a different view, try the Burggraben for the castle walls and glass south wing with the city behind them, or the north bank of the Danube (Urfahr Brückenköpfe) for the castle on its hill with the old town and cathedral.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the castle to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the walls keep their detail. Use the ultra-wide only if nothing important is near the edges, as buildings can look stretched there.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset. The evening light also makes the river look warmer.

text.access_note: The Schlosspark is an open park, but the castle museum and its terraces may have tickets or seasonal limits, so check the official site before you go.

text.description:

The bridge is easiest to photograph as part of its surroundings. Let the line of the roadway lead the eye across the picture, and include whatever foreground is there (ground, bank or water) so the photo feels like a place, not just an object. Switch on the gridlines in your camera app and use them to keep the bridge straight; leaning verticals and a tilted horizon are the most common faults with bridge photos.

If cars or people cross while you are shooting, wait a few seconds for a gap, or use the movement on purpose by taking a few frames in a row and picking the best one. Take one wide shot to show the setting and one closer shot with zoom to pick out the structure itself. Wipe your lens before you start, as a faint film on it can soften the picture, especially when the sun is low.
text.geographic_location: In Linz, about 125 metres north-west of the stand-here point.
text.directions_text: From there the bridge is about 125 metres to the north-west, which is about 2 minutes on foot. Walk towards the bridge, which lies to the north-west. The phone icon on the map is about 120 m south-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from where you stand. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of sky and surroundings, and keep the bridge in the middle of the frame to avoid stretched edges. A 2x or 3x telephoto setting is good for a tighter picture of the structure.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 120 m south-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-west. The bridge lies to the north-west, so face that way with the structure across the frame.

Keep the phone level, leave a strip of foreground (whatever is there, such as ground, bank or water) at the bottom, and let the line of the bridge lead into the picture. Take a wide frame and a zoomed frame so you have a choice later.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the bridge to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so it does not wash out. If you shoot near dusk, try night mode and rest your elbows on a rail or wall to keep the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft light early or late in the day usually suits a bridge, and the blue hour after sunset can look good if the bridge is lit. Midday sun gives harder shadows but still works if you keep the sky in the frame.

name: Old Cathedral, Linz
label: Old Cathedral
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).

notes: Baroque Jesuit church where Anton Bruckner was organist.

text.description: The Old Cathedral (Alter Dom) is a Baroque church in Linz, also known as the Church of Ignatius or the Jesuit Church. The Jesuits built it between 1669 and 1683, and it served as the cathedral of the Diocese of Linz from 1785 until the new cathedral took over in 1909. The outside is fairly plain, which suits a phone photo: two towers with onion domes stand either side of the main door, giving a clear, symmetrical shape that is easy to frame. Inside, the church is richly decorated, with pink marble columns, a carved wooden pulpit and a high altar with many marble statues. Anton Bruckner was organist here from 1856 to 1868, and the Baroque organ he asked to have altered is still in the church. That makes it a nice stop for anyone interested in music as well as architecture. Use the ultra-wide lens to fit the towers in, and keep the phone level so the walls do not lean too much. Step back as far as the space allows, or save a close shot of one tower for the telephoto lens. If you go inside, expect dim light and think about whether photography is welcome during services. Check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: The Old Cathedral is in Linz, at the south end of the Hauptplatz, close to where the former Jesuits' College stood.
text.directions_text: No tram or rail stops are listed for this spot, so head for the Hauptplatz in Linz. Walk to the south end of the square and look for the two onion-domed towers. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x), because you are close to a large building. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer view, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the onion domes.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From there the front of the church and its two towers should fill your frame well, so step back a little if you want more sky and space around them.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the main door with the centre of the frame so the two towers balance on each side. Hold the phone upright and level to keep the walls straight. Include a bit of the street or pavement in front to give a sense of scale. For a second picture, zoom in on one tower and its dome.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or the lightest part of the wall, then lower the exposure slider slightly so the facade keeps its detail. Inside, switch on night mode only if the scene is dark and you can hold still. Otherwise rest your elbows against something steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a bright but soft-lit time of day, when the facade is evenly lit and not in harsh shadow. On a sunny day, check that the sun is not directly behind the towers.

text.access_note: This is a working church, so opening times and photography rules inside may vary. Check the official site before you go.

The distance also lets you choose between a wide view with the surroundings and a closer, tighter shot of the column alone. Start with the default lens (1x) and turn on the gridlines, so you can keep the column upright and the horizon level. Then step back or forward a little and take a second shot with a different amount of sky or surroundings around it. If people are walking through, wait a moment for a gap, or use them to give the picture a sense of scale. Take a few frames with the column off-centre as well as in the middle, then pick your favourite later. For close details, such as details near the top, use the telephoto lens (2x to 5x, depending on your phone) rather than walking right up to the base. It is worth checking each photo for converging lines, since pointing the phone upward makes tall objects lean inward.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole column. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the surroundings in the frame, or to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the top of the column.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 35 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the column up with one of the vertical lines. Keep the phone as upright as you can so the column does not lean. Leave a little space above the top and try one shot with a building or passers-by to show scale.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the column to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail and the sky does not wash out.
